attrs.evidence: probe_execreg_v08_repro.mjs, paired and gating: 2/2 reproduce against a verbatim frozen v0.7.0 — P-2 (registerExecutor('impl-c-derive-…') launches nothing, JS produces every byte, the result is relabelled C, and acceptance returns ok with implementation_provenance 'observed') and P-2b (ONE handle provenances TWO unrelated executions, because a handle binds neither a request nor a set of bytes) — and 5/5 confined against live. derive_realm_battery.mjs 19/19, where cases 11-18 exercise the launch contract end to end: an authority-driven execution reporting all three identities, naming C without launching C, relabelling after observation, a second authority holding no observation for the same bytes, an unnamed artifact refused before spawn, a launcher that declares someone else's files being identified as those files, the naming policy refusing both rebinding directions, and the structural absence of registerExecutor. derive_battery.mjs: in-process-has-no-provenance, requirement-without-observation-refused, no-caller-supplied-provenance, naming-policy-well-formed. grid_check asserts the source-level invariants: accept's exact parameter list, the single writer of the observation table, and that the authority — never the launcher — hashes the artifact.
attrs.revision_note: SUPERSEDED, and it was right about the half it named. @3 said the authority must read and hash the artifact ITSELF rather than believe a name, and that stands. What it did not say is that hashing the declaration establishes nothing about what was then invoked. v0.8.0's launcher carried `artifact_files` (the evidence, honestly hashed) beside `spawn` (an independent caller-controlled action), two fields of one object with nothing binding them — so declaring the genuine JS worker closure, naming that digest as C, and supplying a spawn() that evaluated in-process returned implementation_provenance 'observed' for impl-c-derive with no C anywhere. The same shape held in the film plane against the real C binary's genuine digest. What actually held was 'authority read bytes X, then invoked callback Y'. Frozen as P-3 and P-3F in probe_execlaunch_v09_repro.mjs.
attrs.statement: EXECUTOR EXISTENCE IS NOT EXECUTION PROVENANCE. Proving that an executor exists — even proving which bytes it is made of — says nothing about which bytes came back from which request. An observation must bind the EXECUTOR, the REQUEST and the RETURNED BYTES as one execution event, and acceptance must take no part of that proof from its caller. This is round 17's issuance lesson one level higher: there, don't authenticate the grant, authenticate the WHOLE REQUEST; here, don't authenticate the executor handle, authenticate the WHOLE EXECUTION EVENT. So: manual registration is DELETED; the authority is the thing that runs an executor (execute(req, launcher)); a launcher supplies MECHANISM AND NO IDENTITY — where the artifact's files are and how to start them — and the authority reads and hashes those files itself, resolves the family name from its own digest→name POLICY, spawns, sends that request, takes those bytes, and only then records an observation keyed by H(request_sem_id | canonical(the whole result)); and accept(registry, req, res) consults that privately held table, so a relabelled result MISSES the observation rather than being compared against it. THREE IDENTITIES, because one string was answering three questions: implementation_family_id (what implementation this is), executable_artifact_id (H of the bytes the authority read), and executor_session_id (this particular authority-driven launch). The naming policy is not an observation — it says what bytes are CALLED, never that anything ran — and it is injective in both directions so a caller cannot rewrite it mid-run. DECLARED OPEN, stated conservatively on purpose: hashing a path and then spawning that path supports 'the host observed artifact X immediately before requesting execution of path P'. It is NOT a proof that the OS executed those exact bytes under every filesystem race, and it is not hardware-attested executable identity. Also uncovered: the node binary and standard library for a JS executor, and every shared object the loader binds for a native one.
